title: Intercanopy and Intracanopy Lighting
objective: Evaluate supplemental lighting within or below the canopy by photon redistribution, crop architecture, safety, sanitation, energy, and replicated crop outcomes.

terms.definition: Fixtures positioned between plant rows or canopy zones to deliver light laterally into foliage.
Broad term for fixtures placed within the crop canopy volume.
Fixtures positioned below the main canopy to direct photons upward or into lower tissues.
Photon distribution measured at multiple canopy heights and directions.

coreScience: Secondary lighting can redistribute photons toward shaded leaves and inflorescences. Its value depends on whether it replaces top light at equal total photons or simply adds photons. Trials must distinguish redistribution from increased total photon dose and must measure the vertical and directional profile.

A 2025 medicinal-cannabis study reported increased and more uniform yield under tested subcanopy and inter-canopy systems, but the result belongs to its cultivars, architecture, spectra, dose, layout, and economics. It supports the concept; it does not guarantee the same percentage gain in another room.

Fixtures inside the crop introduce electrical equipment near irrigation, workers, leaves, sprays, and debris. They can obstruct scouting, pruning, movement, sanitation, airflow, and emergency access. Surface temperature, listing, ingress protection, cable routing, cleanability, chemical compatibility, and de-energized service procedures are core design criteria.
cultivationRelevance: The strongest use case is a vertically nonuniform canopy where lower productive tissues remain photon-limited and top intensity cannot rise safely or efficiently.
Success should be judged by saleable yield distribution, uniformity, quality, labor, water use, defects, kilowatt-hours, and total system cost—not yield alone.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Fixture type, position, direction, height, spacing, spectrum, dimming, cable and irrigation relationship.
Top, middle, and lower maps; band; direction; total DLI; replacement versus addition; and control treatment.
Cultivar, density, height, leaf area, training, pruning, and productive-zone definition.
Listing, ingress rating, temperature, cleaning, spray restrictions, access, isolation, and inspection.
Yield and quality by vertical position, CV, water use, labor, defects, kWh, and economic assumptions.

misconceptions: Under-canopy light always adds a fixed yield percentage: Response depends on added photons, architecture, genotype, environment, and baseline distribution.
Lower leaves use any added light efficiently: Age, health, acclimation, orientation, source direction, and sink demand affect response.
Only PPFD matters: Electrical, sanitation, heat, airflow, access, and worker risks can determine whether the system is viable.
evidenceLimits: Cannabis evidence is emerging and includes limited facilities and genotypes. Replicated local trials with equal-photon and energy accounting are needed before broad adoption.
